newsitem.title: USA: Peru's security spending rise won't hurt economy.
newsitem.headline: Peru's security spending rise won't hurt economy.

text.p: Military spending in Peru is expected to rise following the attack by Peruvian rebels late Tuesday on the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, but Latin American debt experts said the increase will not threaten the country's macroeconomic outlook.

"I don't think the overall macro trends are going to change and I think even if they have to increase spending...I would not see it as something that would jeopardize the overall macro outlook," said Joyce Chang, head of emerging markets at Merrill Lynch & Co in New York.

While economists here expect Peru to step up fiscal spending on security, they said the country is probably the most orthodox in Latin America in terms of its economic policies and they do not expect President Alberto Fujimori to change that course.

"The economic implications at this point are not large. I think they are the most orthodox country in Latin America. They have not tinkered with any schemes that would be seen as shortcuts," said Luis R. Luis, head of emerging markets debt at Boston-based investment firm Scudder, Stevens & Clark.

Walter Molano, director of Latin American economic research at SBC Warburg here, agreed saying he did not see any macroeconomic impact at this time. "I think they probably do have the resources to spend more on security."
Indeed, analysts said Peru's impressive economic progress in this decade is largely attributable to the country's very tight fiscal and monetary policies.

According to Morgan Stanley senior Latin American Economist Jaime Valdivia, Peru's inflation has been cut to about 11 percent this year from 11,000 percent in the third quarter of 1990 and the economy has recovered at an average of 7.0 percent during the 1993 to 1996 period.
Still, emerging market experts believe that the political environment in Peru is going to be far more vulnerable in 1997 than had been previously thought.
"I don't think we will see any broad macro trends changing in Peru but we do think that you are set for a year where there will probably be more political noise in 1997," said Chang of Merrill.
Indeed, the outcome of the current hostage crisis is not the only concern for Peru going into 1997.

According to Chang, those who were jailed prior to the implementation of the tough anti-crime and anti-terrorist laws are now up for release and it is something that the special forces will have to deal with in the coming year.
Another factor that will add to Peru's vulnerablility is the ongoing border dispute with neighboring Ecuador.
Talks, scheduled for Friday, were called off Wednesday because of the hostage crisis in Lima, and sources expect the two countries to enter discussions in January.

"Going into January, there will be another round of discussions about the Peru/Ecuador border and you could see some lingering political concerns during that period," said Chang, who does not expect an immediate resolution.
"I think it is something that will not be resolved overnight. It has been going on for 50 years. I think there will be a little noise there this year," she added.
